Proof mechanism.

If W>0W>0, normalize to a cube-valued random vector XX. Let Δ\Delta be the affine determinant of d+1d+1 independent draws. Then

SD⁡(w)=Wd+1(d+1)!​𝔼​|Δ|,𝔼​Δ2=(d+1)!​detCov⁡(X).\operatorname{SD}(w)=\frac{W^{d+1}}{(d+1)!}\mathbb{E}|\Delta|,\qquad\mathbb{E}\Delta^{2}=(d+1)!\det\Cov(X). (S19)

Integrality gives |Δ|≤Δ2|\Delta|\leq\Delta^{2}, while positive semidefiniteness and Hadamard’s inequality give

detCov⁡(X)≤∏iVar⁡(Xi)=W−2​d​∏imi,0​mi,1.\det\Cov(X)\leq\prod_{i}\operatorname{Var}(X_{i})=W^{-2d}\prod_{i}m_{i,0}m_{i,1}. (S20)

Combining the identities and restoring homogeneity proves the inequality. The W=0W=0 case is immediate. Equality requires determinants in {0,±1}\{0,\pm 1\} on positive-probability tuples and diagonal covariance. The supplied formal proof excludes simultaneous equality with all facet masses positive for d≥3d\geq 3, using rational pivots, integer clearing, and a two-level separating construction. A zero facet confines the support to a hyperplane and gives equality directly.

The reported Lean 4.19 chain proves the finite-polynomial inequality and equality characterization, including rejection of an incorrect equality mutation. The relation to the geometric conjecture of Averkov et al. (2026) still requires the complete zonoid/mixed-volume bridge and external statement-alignment review; we do not silently promote the polynomial result to every geometric formulation.

J.1.1 Deriving the determinant second-moment identity

Let Z=(1,X⊤)⊤Z=(1,X^{\top})^{\top} and let Z0,…,ZdZ_{0},\ldots,Z_{d} be independent copies. Write the affine determinant as the determinant of the matrix with these columns. Expanding its square produces a double sum over permutations. Independence lets each term factor into entries of the second-moment matrix G=𝔼⁡[Z​Z⊤]G=\mathbb{E}[ZZ^{\top}]. Regrouping the permutation sums yields

𝔼​det(Z0,…,Zd)2=(d+1)!​detG.\mathbb{E}\det(Z_{0},\ldots,Z_{d})^{2}=(d+1)!\det G. (S21)

The block matrix has the form

G=(1μ⊤μ𝔼⁡[X​X⊤]),μ=𝔼​X.G=\begin{pmatrix}1&\mu^{\top}\\ \mu&\mathbb{E}[XX^{\top}]\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mu=\mathbb{E}X. (S22)

Subtracting the mean contribution through the Schur complement gives detG=det(𝔼⁡[X​X⊤]−μ​μ⊤)=detCov⁡(X)\det G=\det(\mathbb{E}[XX^{\top}]-\mu\mu^{\top})=\det\Cov(X). This establishes the stated identity without requiring a dimension-specific polynomial expansion.

The conversion from the ordered random sample to the unordered simplex polynomial also has a precise multiplicity. Tuples with repeated vertices contribute zero determinant. Each (d+1)(d+1)-element vertex set appears in (d+1)!(d+1)! orders with equal absolute determinant and product weight. Dividing by this factorial is therefore required; omitting it would alter the theorem’s normalization. The powers of WW then restore the degree-2​d2d homogeneous inequality.

J.1.2 Equality requires two simultaneous rigidities

The integrality step is sharp exactly when every positive-probability determinant has absolute value zero or one. The covariance step is sharp when the relevant covariance matrix satisfies the equality condition of Hadamard’s inequality. If a facet mass is zero, the support lies in a coordinate hyperplane, so all full-dimensional determinants vanish and both sides are zero.

The difficult direction is excluding equality when all facet masses are positive in dimension at least three. The first inequality constrains affine determinants of the support, while the second constrains its mixed moments. Neither condition alone excludes many nondegenerate distributions. The formal equality argument connects them through the supplied rational-pivot and separator construction. This is a separate proof component, not an automatic corollary of writing down the covariance inequality.

The low-dimensional cases are deliberately outside the stated d≥3d\geq 3 iff classification. The inequality holds for all positive dimensions, but equality can have a different structure in dimensions one and two. Preserving the dimension qualifier prevents a true general inequality from carrying an overgeneralized equality statement.

J.1.3 Formal statement alignment and geometric interpretation

The Lean result checks a finite polynomial built from cube vertices, weights, and determinant coefficients. The source geometric question involves zonoids and mixed-volume formulations. Even if the finite inequality is the central algebraic obstruction, transferring the formal theorem to an external geometric claim requires the exact reduction, its normalization, and its hypotheses. A proof assistant cannot fill that bridge merely because both discussions use the word “Hypercube.”

This case therefore has two distinct strengths: a short reusable proof mechanism for the inequality, and a reported complete formal chain for the finite statement including equality. Its remaining external gate is alignment and priority, rather than an unproved finite polynomial calculation. That status differs substantially from the kernel-only formalizations in the later analytic cases.

J.2.1 From a combinatorial object to a Hilbert-series counterexample

The counterexample begins with a matroid, not with an arbitrary proposed coefficient sequence. A sequence violating front-loading is relevant only if it is produced by the radial construction applied to a valid matroid. The verifier therefore starts with the subset-rank function and checks the matroid axioms before building the graded operators. The 512-subset domain is exhaustive for a nine-element ground set.

Rank normalization, monotonicity, and submodularity serve different purposes. Normalization fixes the empty-set rank and basic bounds; monotonicity controls inclusions; submodularity ensures the rank function has the required exchange structure. Simplicity excludes loops and parallel elements under the stated convention. The independent basis reconstruction checks that the resulting combinatorial object agrees with the reported 67 bases rather than only with a cached list of flats.

The algebraic stage builds rational atom spaces and the radial lowering operator. Its exact column-space recursion computes dimensions, which are integers but can be sensitive to a single omitted operator or an incorrect cover relation. Floating rank estimates near singularity would be inappropriate here. Exact rational arithmetic and the formal finite calculation support the displayed H0H_{0}, HβH_{\beta}, and their difference.

J.3.3 What an exact positivity certificate must establish

A rational certificate has three independent obligations. First, reconstruct the correct numerator from the original functional after clearing only denominators known to be positive in the chart. Second, prove the chart and its inequalities cover the assigned boundary region. Third, expand the proposed nonnegative blocks exactly and show that their sum equals that numerator. Positive coefficients in a polynomial produced by an incorrect substitution would not establish the theorem.

The supplied boundary proof separates zero-off-diagonal and zero-diagonal faces, then treats bounded algebraic regions and an unbounded spectral tail. The detailed sizes quoted earlier concern the zero-diagonal branch, not every face. The lower threshold LL and upper threshold UU satisfy U−L=u⁡(1−u)​r2≥0U-L=u(1-u)r^{2}\geq 0 in the registered nonnegative chart, so the middle interval is well ordered. Coverage at u=0,1u=0,1 and other degenerate denominators must be handled by the branch contract rather than silently removed.

Weighted pairings and Bernstein transformations are certificates only after exact reconstruction. Floating optimization may find promising nonnegative block coefficients; rationalization can change identities or positivity. The independent expansion and deleted-pairing control check precisely this transition from a numerical proposal to an exact object. Full Lean reflection of these large branch certificates is still outstanding.

J.4.1 Why the interpolation family has exactly the required size

There are (n+d−2n−1)=q\binom{n+d-2}{n-1}=q subsets II of size n−1n-1, matching the dimension of homogeneous degree-d−1d-1 forms in nn variables. Each HIH_{I} also has degree d−1d-1, because its product contains d−1d-1 omitted tt indices. The diagonal evaluation matrix HI​(vJ)H_{I}(v_{J}) therefore witnesses interpolation rather than merely supplying many candidate linear forms.

If I≠JI\neq J have equal size, some index in JJ is absent from II. That index occurs in the product defining HIH_{I}, and the partial-fraction identity makes the corresponding factor vanish at vJv_{J}. On the diagonal, the pairwise-distinct parameter condition prevents the necessary factors from vanishing. This explains the off-diagonal zero pattern and the nonzero diagonal without relying on a finite symbolic example.

The basis property of ℓId−1\ell_{I}^{d-1} lets the Xα​YαX_{\alpha}Y^{\alpha} target be expressed in the tangent span of the ddth powers. The constant identity then cancels the degree-zero part. The field must allow the scalar operations and degree factors used in the tangent construction; the displayed Waring statement is therefore made in characteristic zero rather than casually transferred to small characteristic.

J.4.2 Flattening lower bound and ordinary rank are different arguments

The first derivative space of Bn,dB_{n,d} has dimension q+nq+n. Derivatives with respect to the XX variables span all degree-d−1d-1 monomials in YY. Derivatives with respect to the YY variables have positive XX degree and are independent through the distinguished terms specified above. The two subspaces have different XX degrees and intersect trivially. A rank-one symmetric tensor contributes at most one dimension to this flattening, so the dimension gives a border-rank lower bound.

That lower bound does not produce the larger ordinary Waring rank d​qdq. Ordinary rank needs the stronger product-space argument. In any proposed decomposition, vanishing second derivatives in the XX variables creates algebraic relations among coordinatewise products of coefficient vectors. The retained Schur–Kneser proof organizes these relations by stabilizer blocks and sums the resulting block lower bounds. Its dependencies and equality hypotheses require specialist verification; the binary tangent identity alone cannot establish the lower bound.

The upper ordinary-rank construction uses a different count: each of the qq tangent monomials is expressed using dd powers, yielding d​qdq terms. Matching this explicit upper bound with the independent lower bound yields equality. Distinguishing the two proofs prevents the border construction from being mistaken for a finite exact decomposition of length q+nq+n.

Substitution into the binomial expansion leaves exactly

Limit mechanism and controls.

Complete Galois packets combine all central orders. Small dd use a nonzero integer norm for a lower bound; large dd use main-term dominance and root-of-unity spacing. Uniform normalized error estimates then supply the asserted limit. These analytic estimates are a necessary proof layer; finite determinant agreement alone does not establish convergence.

Follow-up chain classifications, nonconvergence constructions, and cofinal recovery claims remain within this specialist research line; the current manuscript does not treat them as additional independent discoveries.

J.5.1 Regular-representation multiplicities and determinant products

The finite quotient has order q3q^{3}. Its regular representation contains each irreducible representation with multiplicity equal to its dimension. Therefore an irreducible packet determinant must be raised to that multiplicity when reconstructing the full determinant. The identity ∑d|qφ⁡(d)​n2​d2=q3\sum_{d\mid q}\varphi(d)n^{2}d^{2}=q^{3} checks the dimension accounting, but a complete reconstruction must also ensure that the packets are neither omitted nor duplicated.

Writing 𝒫d\mathcal{P}_{d} for the packets of exact central order dd and Δd,u,v=1−md​(u−v)\Delta_{d,u,v}=1-m^{d}(u-v), the regular determinant has the product form

|detAm,q|=∏d|q∏(u,v)∈𝒫d|Δd,u,v|d.|\det A_{m,q}|=\prod_{d\mid q}\prod_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{P}_{d}}|\Delta_{d,u,v}|^{d}. (S47)

Consequently its normalized logarithm is

log⁡Dq​(Am)=1q3​∑d|qd​∑(u,v)∈𝒫dlog⁡|1−md​(u−v)|.\log D_{q}(A_{m})=\frac{1}{q^{3}}\sum_{d\mid q}d\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{P}_{d}}\log|1-m^{d}(u-v)|. (S48)

This formula identifies exactly what the limit proof must control: packet multiplicities, the main d​log⁡md\log m contribution, and the logarithmic error caused by possible proximity of u−vu-v to m−dm^{-d}.

The scalar identity det(I−m​T)=1−md​(u−v)\det(I-mT)=1-m^{d}(u-v) simplifies each packet dramatically. It does not itself determine how frequently a given (d,u,v)(d,u,v) occurs. This is why packet algebra and representation classification are listed as separate verification layers. Incorrect multiplicities can preserve each packet identity while giving the wrong normalized finite determinant and limiting exponent.

The reverse characteristic polynomial is convenient because it encodes det(I−z​T)\det(I-zT) directly. If it equals 1−c​zd1-cz^{d}, substituting z=mz=m proves the packet formula. The Lean kernel formalizes this algebraic implication. The quantum-binomial relation and vanishing lower traces are the mathematical route to its hypothesis in the registered representation family; they remain to be connected formally for the full theorem.

J.5.2 Why exact finite controls do not establish the limit

Agreement between direct integer determinants and resultants at q≤9q\leq 9 tests packet reconstruction, signs, and normalization in concrete cases. It cannot prove convergence as i→∞i\to\infty. A limiting formula needs an error estimate that remains valid over all packets and all levels in the chain. Near-cancellation in factors of the form 1−md​(u−v)1-m^{d}(u-v) is especially relevant after taking logarithms.

The retained proof divides the packets into small and large central orders. Complete Galois products at small orders are nonzero integers, giving a lower bound that would not be available for an isolated small complex factor. At large orders, dominant terms and spacing among roots of unity control the normalized error. The cutoff and uniform estimates are part of the analytic proof, not parameters chosen to fit the finite determinant values.

More explicitly, choose a cutoff D=D⁡(q)D=D(q) with D→∞D\to\infty and D=o⁡(q)D=o(q). For d≤Dd\leq D, combine every Galois orbit before taking logarithms. Nonvanishing of the resulting integer norm prevents an individual near-zero complex factor from producing an uncontrolled negative contribution; the total small-order contribution is o⁡(q3)o(q^{3}) after normalization. For d>Dd>D, factor

1−md​(u−v)=md​(u−v)​(1−1md​(u−v)).1-m^{d}(u-v)=m^{d}(u-v)\left(1-\frac{1}{m^{d}(u-v)}\right). (S49)

The first factor supplies d​log⁡md\log m plus the root-of-unity term log⁡|u−v|\log|u-v|. The spacing estimate controls the latter after complete packet summation, while m−dm^{-d} makes the last logarithm uniformly summable away from the paired zero modes. Under the retained packet-counting lemma, the coefficient of log⁡m\log m converges to 1/(p+1)1/(p+1) and every residual sum is o⁡(1)o(1) after division by q3q^{3}. Exponentiating therefore gives Dq​(Am)→m1/(p+1)D_{q}(A_{m})\to m^{1/(p+1)}.

Taking logarithms of the claimed limit gives (log⁡m)/(p+1)(\log m)/(p+1), while the infinite determinant has logarithm log⁡m\log m. Their difference is p​log⁡m/(p+1)p\log m/(p+1). This elementary consequence makes the size of the defect explicit but does not replace the convergence argument. It also emphasizes chain dependence: a different quotient chain may have a different packet distribution and a different limit or no limit.

J.5.3 Sign conventions and specialist review

The negative even-level determinant −735-735 is a useful convention check. A normalized determinant intended to compare with a positive Fuglede–Kadison determinant must use the registered absolute or appropriate singular-value convention. Copying the odd-order packet formula into an even-level test without adjusting its hypotheses would be a separate error. The manuscript reports the even controls precisely to make such convention failures visible.

The source counterexample demonstrates the failure of determinant approximation. The exact limit and chain classifications are subsequent results that call for an independent operator-algebraic analysis. Although the formal determinant identity provides substantial and reusable evidence, the principal analytical challenge lies beyond the identity itself.

J.6.3 Finite optimality, family asymptotics, and global extremality

The Arb calculations address the frozen finite optimization problem through horizon 5,000, using outward rounding so that numerical comparisons are certified as intervals. The two implementations reduce the chance of a shared dynamic-programming error. Their agreement on a finite range does not show that the alternating family is globally optimal at every larger size.

The asymptotic statement concerns the alternating family itself. Even a complete proof of that family recurrence and its limit would not establish that no other family has a smaller limiting objective. The global extremal question requires a comparison principle over all allowed permutations or trees. The manuscript keeps these three levels distinct: finite certified comparisons, the family’s analytic expansion, and the unresolved all-family extremality claim.

The second-order finite estimates approaching sinh2⁡(u∗)/(6​cosh⁡(u∗))≈0.11\sinh^{2}(u_{*})/(6\cosh(u_{*}))\approx 0.11 are consistency checks at the β\sqrt{\beta} scale. The separate coefficient sinh2⁡(u∗)/6≈0.16\sinh^{2}(u_{*})/6\approx 0.16 belongs to the β\beta scale. Keeping the exact symbolic expressions alongside two-decimal approximations prevents those two coefficients from being conflated.

Their independent representations help detect normalization or cyclotomic arithmetic errors. An exceptional prime in the norm support means the sufficient lifting conclusion is unavailable there; it should not automatically be described as a proved singular case.

K.6 ERG(3,8): cycle spectrum and factor-criticality

Conditional on completeness and correctness of the frozen 477,142-record catalogue, every listed triangle-free 27-vertex graph with independence number at most seven has cycles of every length from 4 through 27 and is factor-critical. Here factor-criticality means that deleting any vertex leaves a graph with a perfect matching, consisting of 13 edges in this case.

The primary pass constructs cycles and vertex-deleted matchings. The independent pass uses generic cycle enumeration and a skew Tutte matrix over 𝔽2147483647\mathbb{F}_{2147483647}. Rank 26 with a full-support kernel gives the required nonvanishing principal cofactors in the odd-order skew setting, which certifies the vertex-deleted matching condition under the checker theorem. The finite-field certificate is a witness of nonvanishing, not an inference from a failed search for a matching.

K.7 Kasami APN counting identity at n equal to fourteen

For admissible kk with gcd⁡(k,14)=1\gcd(k,14)=1, the retained finite result verifies the source NSUCRYPTO counting identity for the Kasami power F⁡(x)=x4k−2k+1F(x)=x^{4^{k}-2^{k}+1} over GF⁡(214)\mathrm{GF}(2^{14}). Frobenius symmetry reduces the new representative computations to k=3k=3 and k=5k=5.

Two different irreducible-polynomial field models check 16,382 admissible ρ\rho values per representative, giving 32,764 exact identities Z⁡(ρ)=0Z(\rho)=0 in the source notation. Both derivative images have 8,192 elements with two-point fibers, and the reported Walsh support has size 3,088.

The formula defining ZZ and the symmetry reduction are part of the source problem and must be included with a standalone certificate release. The present evidence extends a finite verified boundary from n≤13n\leq 13 to n=14n=14. It does not establish an arbitrary-nn counting theorem or a new general APN construction. The work illustrates exact finite algebra at a new parameter boundary with representation-independent checks.

K.8 ReLU MAX8 certificate compression and subset-profile dynamic programming

Starting from the public four-template MAX6 certificate, the local attachment search contains 676 raw candidates, 127 graph-isomorphism classes, and 125 exact function columns. The retained combination yields a 25-template degree-three MAX8 identity. The source’s public 69-template certificate expands to 515,488 symmetric second-layer atoms, whereas the retained certificate uses 187,460: a reported 63.63% reduction and 2.75-fold compression.

Full 8!8! permutation enumeration and subset-profile dynamic programming agree term by term. The dynamic program aggregates permutations according to profiles sufficient for the certificate evaluation, so its correctness requires proving that aggregated transitions preserve every evaluated contribution. Agreement on a complete finite instance checks that reduction against brute-force enumeration.

The same generic verifier checks public MAXN certificates for 5≤N≤105\leq N\leq 10, reducing the largest replay from approximately 1.46 billion permutations to 71.77 million transitions. This is a verification-efficiency result as well as a compressed certificate.

K.9 AES CNOT Pareto cleanup

A separate local rewrite begins with the source 20-qubit AES circuit containing 44 Toffoli gates and 197 CNOT gates. Two identical CNOT pairs can commute through intervening gates and cancel, giving 193 CNOT gates while preserving all 44 Toffolis. The two retained commutation windows span 22 and 23 gates, and the independent verifier checks all 47 intervening commutations recorded by the certificate.

All 256 input cases pass the independent truth-table check. This validates the finite circuit transformation under the registered input and ancilla contract. It is a modest Pareto improvement: one gate type decreases while the dominant Toffoli count stays fixed. It is distinct from the Hyperfactor cross-output construction and should not be added to its T-count savings as though both changes were applied to the same baseline.

Separate exhaustive single-delete and 10,920 two-delete/one-insert affine charts do not reduce the eight-Toffoli count of the four-bit inverse. Those search negatives prove only absence within the explored rewrite neighborhoods. They are not a global Toffoli lower bound.

K.10 Factorwise tail elimination for transferred tensors

For st333, EPOCH identified a retained optimizer in which one derivative mode vanishes in each of ten rank-one terms, eliminating the cubic derivative product. An exhaustive search over all 310=59,0493^{10}=59{,}049 mode patterns found 1,536 admissible realizations; the selected path has coefficient weights (0,18,8,0)(0,18,8,0) and gives

R⁡(T⊗N)≤(N+1)​10N.R(T^{\otimes N})\leq(N+1)10^{N}. (S65)

Under the supplied scalar-count model, this lowers the crossover with exact rank-11 recursion from N=48N=48 to N=39N=39, and the crossover with explicit base-field recursion from N=90N=90 to N=81N=81.

The same mechanism transfers to ss333 and to the 35-term st555 construction. For st555, the coefficient weights become (0,75,922,0)(0,75,922,0), improving the two reported crossover thresholds from (41,78)(41,78) to (33,70)(33,70). This session shows how EPOCH can convert a structural observation about a border construction into a measurable reduction in exactification overhead.

K.11 Degree-eight Smale reductions

EPOCH reduced the nearest-critical-point problem to a one-variable polynomial problem on the unit disk using the Grace–Walsh–Szegő theorem. Exact Schur and Sturm certificates then establish

|P⁡(b)b|>4335000≈0.09,\left|\frac{P(b)}{b}\right|>\frac{433}{5000}\approx 0.09, (S66)

which improves the corresponding general-degree estimate at degree eight by a factor of approximately 4.314.31 under the same normalization.

The analysis also isolates the multiple-critical-point case and proves the sharp bound

|P⁡(b)b|≥18,\left|\frac{P(b)}{b}\right|\geq\frac{1}{8}, (S67)

with equality attained by [1−(1−z)8]/8[1-(1-z)^{8}]/8. The session combines a classical reduction with exact region certification, yielding both a stronger numerical bound and a sharper structural description of any remaining counterexample.

K.12 A cofinite unfair-trinomial family

EPOCH turned a finite recurrence pattern into a parameter-uniform obstruction. For every integer k≥3,000,001k\geq 3{,}000{,}001 with gcd⁡(k,3)=1\gcd(k,3)=1 and every 0<a<10<a<1, no nonzero polynomial with nonnegative coefficients can multiply

1+a​x3+xk1+ax^{3}+x^{k} (S68)

into a polynomial whose coefficients all belong to {0,1}\{0,1\}.

The proof organizes the recurrence into three residue classes and controls the resulting negative-binomial packets through projective contraction, seam estimates, an antiperiodic theta kernel, and a terminal recurrence. Exact symbolic and rational replays verify the algebraic identities used throughout. This case illustrates EPOCH’s capacity to recognize a computational pattern, identify the mechanism behind it, and promote it to an explicit theorem for an infinite family.

Global monotonicity is certified by 6,615 positive ordered Bernstein controls, 13,140 positive ratio controls, and a reduced derivative certificate with 14 positive controls. A complementary sharp-stability argument is represented by 31,765 rational nonnegative blocks. This session demonstrates EPOCH’s ability to organize a large exact certificate into a transparent quantitative theorem with a sharp equality case.

Across these sessions, the advantage of EPOCH is not the volume of computations performed, but the conversion of search output into reusable mathematical structure: optimized constructions, exact inequalities, uniform parameter arguments, and independently replayable certificates.
